sentence: A penicillin-type antibiotic, available on prescription, used for infections of the skin and wounds, bone infections and ear infections.
note: NHS about page: penicillin antibiotic, prescription only, skin/wound, bone (osteomyelitis) and ear infections.

sentence: It is not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to a penicillin, and a serious allergic reaction is an emergency that needs a 999 call.
note: NHS who-can page lists past penicillin allergy; side effects page says anaphylaxis is an emergency, call 999.

sentence: Rarely it can affect the liver, sometimes after the course has ended.
note: NHS side effects page and emc leaflet: liver effects can be delayed for up to two months.

note: NHS about page: it kills the bacteria causing the infection.

sentence: As a penicillin, it works by damaging the cell wall that bacteria need to survive, which human cells do not have.
note: Plain textbook statement about beta-lactam action.

sentence: Antibiotics act on bacteria, so they do not treat illnesses caused by viruses.
For most infections the NHS says people usually feel better within a few days.
note: Search summary of NHS about/how-to-take pages; the blended summary did not say which page carried it.

sentence: Feeling sick and diarrhoea are the main common effects, with bloating and indigestion; the NHS says these affect more than 1 in 100 people.
Simple meals and small sips of fluid are suggested by the NHS to help with an upset stomach and to avoid dehydration.
Being sick can mean the combined pill or the progestogen-only pill does not protect against pregnancy.
Rarely, anaphylaxis (swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, severe breathing difficulty or fainting) is an emergency that needs a 999 call.
Yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes with pale stools and dark urine can signal liver problems; the NHS says to contact a GP or NHS 111 promptly.
note: NHS side effects page: serious side effects, rare (fewer than 1 in 10,000), call a doctor or 111.

sentence: Bloody or mucus-containing diarrhoea, blistering or peeling skin, unusual bruising, or joint or muscle pain starting a couple of days into treatment also need a GP or NHS 111 contact.
Some serious effects, including liver effects, can appear for up to two months after treatment has finished.
note: NHS side effects page and emc leaflet (delayed up to 2 months).

sentence: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to flucloxacillin, another penicillin-type antibiotic or any other medicine as a reason to check with a doctor or pharmacist first.
People with liver or kidney problems, and people who have recently had or are due a vaccination, are also listed for checking first.
Liver injury such as jaundice or hepatitis is a recognised risk; the NHS formulary says it is higher with longer courses and increasing age.
note: emc leaflet (jaundice, hepatitis) and NHS formulary summary (longer courses, age); search summary blended these.

sentence: It can make the oral typhoid vaccine less effective.
Medicines to check about include methotrexate, warfarin, gout medicines such as probenecid, voriconazole and other antibiotics.
There is not enough information to say herbal remedies and supplements are free of interaction with it.
Very rarely, taking it with paracetamol has been linked to a blood and fluid imbalance (high anion gap metabolic acidosis).
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking it.
note: NHS common questions page via search summary.

sentence: NHS England directions note that INR is checked during treatment in people taking warfarin or similar anticoagulants, because INR rises have been reported.
note: NHS England PGD via search summary (INR rises reported with warfarin).

sentence: Capsules and, in the sources, an oral liquid and injection forms.
note: NHS page and emc leaflets (capsules; powder for injection); oral solution inferred from NHS PGD titles.

sentence: Flucloxacillin is a penicillin-type antibiotic, and the NHS says it is available only on prescription.
It is used to treat infections of the skin and wounds, bone infections known as osteomyelitis, and ear infections.
In England, community pharmacists can also supply it for some skin problems, such as impetigo and infected insect bites, under NHS patient group directions.
Antibiotics act on bacteria, so they do not help illnesses caused by viruses.
The NHS says that for most infections people usually feel better within a few days.
It notes that completing the prescribed course helps stop the infection coming back.
note: Blended search summary: finishing the course helps stop the infection returning.

sentence: Flucloxacillin is one of several penicillin antibiotics, and the NHS groups penicillins together as widely used for skin, dental, throat and chest infections.
note: NHS wording as reported by search summary; it did not tie flucloxacillin itself to chest infections.

sentence: According to the NHS, flucloxacillin works by killing the bacteria that cause the infection.
As a penicillin, it acts on the cell wall that bacteria need to stay intact, a structure human cells do not have.
note: Plain textbook statement about beta-lactam action.

sentence: Because it is a penicillin, it sits in the same family as amoxicillin.
note: NHS groups flucloxacillin with other penicillins.

sentence: This shared family is why the NHS asks about any past allergic reaction to a penicillin-type antibiotic before it is used.
note: NHS who-can page lists penicillin-type allergy.

sentence: UK patient leaflets say it should not be taken by people with an allergy to penicillin or other antibiotics of the same kind.
note: emc leaflets via search summary (penicillin or beta-lactam allergy).

sentence: UK leaflets describe itchy rash, sore mouth or eyes, swelling of the face, lips, throat or tongue, and breathing problems as signs of a severe allergic reaction, and swelling or breathing difficulty is a reason for a 999 call.
note: emc leaflets via search summary; NHS side effects page for 999.

sentence: The NHS describes flucloxacillin as best absorbed on an empty stomach, meaning it is taken before eating or a good while after a meal or snack.
note: NHS about page via search summary (empty stomach, an hour before or two hours after food).

sentence: Capsules are swallowed whole with a full glass of water, and the NHS advises against lying down straight after.
note: NHS main page via search summary.

sentence: The medicine comes as capsules, and UK leaflets also describe a powder made up into an injection.
note: NHS main page and emc leaflets (powder for injection).

sentence: Even when symptoms improve within a few days, the NHS describes completing the prescribed course as the way to help stop the infection coming back.
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk during treatment.
note: NHS common questions page via search summary.

sentence: The number of doses each day and the length of the course are set by the prescriber and printed on the pharmacy label, so they are not listed here.
note: Descriptive statement that dosing is in the NHS page and leaflet; no figures given.

sentence: The NHS says most adults and children can take flucloxacillin, with a few exceptions to check first.
These include a past allergic reaction to flucloxacillin, another penicillin-type antibiotic or any other medicine.
People with liver or kidney problems, and those who have recently had or are due a vaccination, are also on the list.
In pregnancy the NHS says it can be taken, but a pharmacist or doctor is asked first.
UK product information adds that it is used in pregnancy only when the benefit outweighs the risk.
For breastfeeding, the NHS says only tiny amounts pass into breast milk, so side effects in the baby are unlikely.
note: NHS pregnancy/breastfeeding page via search summary.

sentence: A baby who has poor feeding, vomiting, diarrhoea, thrush or a rash is a reason to call NHS 111 if a parent is worried.
note: NHS main page via search summary.

sentence: The NHS says common side effects, affecting more than 1 in 100 people, are feeling sick, diarrhoea, bloating and indigestion.
Simple meals and small sips of fluid are suggested to avoid dehydration, and being sick can reduce the protection of the contraceptive pill.
Serious side effects are rare, affecting fewer than 1 in 10,000 people according to the NHS.
They include yellowing of the skin or eyes with pale stools and dark urine, which can point to liver problems.
UK leaflets describe jaundice and hepatitis, meaning liver inflammation, as effects that can be delayed for up to two months after treatment ends.
An NHS formulary says the liver risk is higher with longer courses and with increasing age.
note: BSW NHS formulary via search summary.

sentence: Bloody or mucus-containing diarrhoea, blistering or peeling skin, unusual bruising, and joint or muscle pain starting a couple of days in are also warning signs.
For these, the NHS says to contact a doctor or NHS 111, and some can appear after the course has finished.
Anaphylaxis is rare but an emergency, with swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, severe breathing difficulty or fainting needing a 999 call.
The NHS says some medicines can change how flucloxacillin works or raise the chance of side effects.
Examples it names are methotrexate, warfarin, gout medicines such as probenecid, voriconazole and other antibiotics.
Flucloxacillin can make the oral typhoid vaccine less effective, so a doctor is told about a recent or planned vaccine.
NHS England directions note that INR rises have been reported in people on warfarin or similar anticoagulants, who therefore have INR checked.
note: NHS England PGD via search summary.

sentence: Very rarely, a blood and fluid imbalance called high anion gap metabolic acidosis has been reported when it is taken with paracetamol.
The NHS says there is not enough information to say herbal remedies and supplements are free of interaction, partly because they are usually not tested for their effect on other medicines.
The NHS lists are examples only, and the leaflet in the pack has the full list.
The NHS describes it as taken on an empty stomach, which means before eating or well after a meal or snack.
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk during treatment, though it also lists liver problems as a possible rare side effect worth knowing about.
note: NHS common questions page and side effects page.

sentence: Swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, severe breathing difficulty or fainting is a medical emergency, and the NHS says to call 999 straight away.

UK leaflets and the NHS say serious effects, including jaundice or hepatitis, can appear up to two months after finishing, so yellow skin or eyes with pale stools and dark urine needs a GP or NHS 111 contact.
note: NHS side effects page and emc leaflet.
